beats.role_note: The mechanism before the build — R point on the cell cycle
beats.narration_text: The restriction point is the cell cycle's point of no return. Early in G1, the cell is still checking: are conditions good enough to divide? This plate animates the same stimulus — growth factor withdrawal — applied to two cells at different positions on the loop.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — clockwise circle (cell cycle loop); VERM gate square at ten-o-clock; two BLUE cell circles on the loop (one at 234°, one at 186°); radial outward arrows from each

beats.role_note: Stakes before the build — position decides fate
beats.narration_text: Before the restriction point, withdrawal means exit — the cell slides off the loop and waits. After it, withdrawal means nothing — the cell has already committed to dividing no matter what signals come next. One gate, two completely opposite outcomes.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — pre-gate cell exits loop (arrow pointing outward); post-gate cell stays on loop (arrow retracts); annotation: 'same stimulus, opposite fate — position decides'

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL B05_RestrictionPoint class, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it. The loop is a Circle — GRAY, stroke only, no fill. The gate is a Square at the two-ten position: cosine and sine of that angle scale the radius, then move underscore to places it on the arc. The two cells are Circles at two-thirty-four and one-eighty-six degrees, same math. The radial arrows point from cell centre outward at that angle — direction is the same vector as the position. Four plays: Create the loop, FadeIn the gate, LaggedStart the cells, GrowArrow both arrows, then Flash the gate.

props.title: scenes.py — B05_RestrictionPoint
props.code:
# scenes.py — Claude Code output
import math
BLUE="#0072B2"; VERM="#D55E00"; GRAY="#7c7c7c"
R=2.8   # loop radius

def pos(deg):
    a=math.radians(deg)
    return np.array([R*math.cos(a), R*math.sin(a), 0])

class B05_RestrictionPoint(Scene):
  def construct(self):
    loop=Circle(radius=R,color=GRAY,stroke_width=3.5)
    ga=210
    gate=Square(side_length=0.45,color=VERM,fill_color=VERM,
      fill_opacity=0.5,stroke_width=3).move_to(pos(ga))
    cells=[]
    arrows=[]
    for deg in (234,186):
      p=pos(deg)
      cells.append(Circle(radius=0.30,color=BLUE,
        fill_color=BLUE,fill_opacity=0.2,
        stroke_width=3).move_to(p))
      d=p/np.linalg.norm(p)
      arrows.append(Arrow(p,p+d*0.9,buff=0.28,
        color=GRAY,stroke_width=2.8,
        max_tip_length_to_length_ratio=0.22))
    self.play(Create(loop),run_time=0.8)
    self.play(FadeIn(gate,scale=1.2),run_time=0.4)
    self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(c) for c in cells],
              lag_ratio=0.3,run_time=0.7))
    self.play(*[GrowArrow(a) for a in arrows],run_time=0.6)
    self.play(Flash(gate.get_center(),color=VERM,
              line_length=0.25,num_lines=12,flash_radius=0.55))
    self.wait(0.8)

beats.role_note: Manim render of B05_RestrictionPoint — loop, gate, two cells, radial arrows, Flash
beats.narration_text: Run it. The loop draws in. The gate appears — a small vermillion square near ten-o-clock. Two blue cells fade in, one before the gate, one after. Both outward arrows grow simultaneously. The Flash fires on the gate. That gate square is the entire plot — everything that happens next depends on which side of it you are standing.

The change. Revise: after revealing both cells, animate their fate. Pre-gate cell moves off the loop radially — it exits. Post-gate cell's arrow retracts — it is committed. Flash the gate square to show that position on the loop is everything.

props.command:
claude "Revise: after revealing both cells, animate their fate.
Pre-gate cell moves off the loop radially (exits). Post-gate cell's arrow
retracts — it's committed. Flash the gate square to show position decides fate."

beats.role_note: Manim render of B07_RestrictionPointFate — pre-gate exits, post-gate committed
beats.narration_text: Watch the revision. Both cells are on the loop. Then fate kicks in. The pre-gate cell moves off — it leaves the loop in the direction of its outward arrow. The post-gate cell's arrow retracts — no exit available. The gate flashes again. Same gate, same moment, two cells, two different futures. The animation makes the spatial distinction physical.

The gate's position on the loop is everything. Two identical cells, one identical signal, two opposite fates. The animation made that spatial distinction visible. Claude ported the loop geometry, placed the gate at the right angle, placed two cells, and drew radial arrows in one prompt. The revision animated the divergence — one cell exits, one commits.
beats.visual_intent: Slate — summary card: 'position = fate'; loop diagram with pre-gate cell exiting and post-gate cell staying; annotation: 'R point: past this, no going back'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud AND discussed. greeting = 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt into Claude: add a third cell at position one-eighty degrees — exactly at the gate — and show it paused, undecided. Then animate a coin-flip: the third cell randomly moves either forward past the gate or backward off the loop. Why run it? Because at the gate itself, the decision is probabilistic — noise in the Rb phosphorylation state determines which way it tips. The animation can show that stochasticity as a branching event rather than a clean binary.

props.command:
claude "Add a third cell at 210°, exactly at the gate — paused, pulsing.
Then animate it branching: 50% chance forward (committed), 50% backward (exits).
Show the gate as a probabilistic switch, not a clean binary."
